title: Goosegrass in Rice Fields: How to Spot It and Control It
metaTitle: Goosegrass in Rice: How to Identify and Control It
metaDescription: Goosegrass makes about 50,000 seeds a plant and hosts blast and sheath blight. Learn how to spot this tough grass weed and keep it off your palay.
excerpt: Goosegrass is a tough, clumping grass weed of rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. It hugs the ground in a flat tuft and sends up spikes shaped like fingers. Besides taking food from your palay, it hosts three rice diseases. This page shows how to spot it, why it matters and how to control it.

blocks.text:
Goosegrass (Eleusine indica) is a common member of the grass family. It carries many local names, including bakis bakisan, bang angan, bikad bikad, bila bila, palagtiki, parangis, paragis, sabung sabungan and sambali. In rice farming, it shows up in rainfed lowland fields, where water does not always stand in the paddy. You will often see it on paths and bunds around the farm too.

This weed is an annual. It lives for one season and spreads only by seed. But each plant makes a huge number of seeds. Besides that, animals that eat the seed heads carry the seeds to new places. So one clump left to ripen on a bund can seed a whole field.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about goosegrass
rows: Bakis bakisan, bang angan, bikad bikad, bila bila, palagtiki, parangis, paragis, sabung sabungan, sambali

blocks.text: This weed grows as a smooth, flat tuft that spreads low and then rises. Like any grass, it has jointed stems with clear nodes, but its stems look flat rather than round. The stem base is whitish, turning pale green higher up. Leaf blades are flat, narrow and hairy on top, with long hairs where blade meets sheath. The ligule is a thin membrane, and there are no auricles. At the top, 3 to 6 spikes fan out like fingers.

items: A flat, smooth tuft hugs the ground, with stems spreading out from the center.
Stem bases look whitish, and the color fades to pale green higher up.
Long hairs sit where the leaf blade joins the sheath, and auricles are missing.
The collar of the leaf sheath is moderately hairy, and the ligule is a thin membrane.
Seed heads end in a whorl of 3 to 6 spikes that spread like fingers.
Look alike tip: crowfoot grass has short, thick finger spikes, while these spikes are long and slender.

blocks.text:
Goosegrass is a C4 weed, so it grows strongly in full sun and heat. Each plant makes 50,000 seeds on average. Animals that eat the seed heads also spread those seeds with ease. As a result, a few plants can seed a large area.

No report yet shows how strongly it competes with rice. Even so, it uses the same water, light and fertilizer that your palay needs. Its bigger threat is disease. It is an alternative host of Rhizoctonia solani, which causes sheath blight, and Pyricularia oryzae, which causes blast. It also hosts Sarocladium oryzae, which causes sheath rot.

items: Keep the bunds and paths around your paddy clean, since this grass often grows there first and then seeds into the field.
Keep water standing in the field when you can. This grass prefers drier ground and does poorly under flooding.
Pull clumps on wet soil before the finger spikes ripen. Its roots grip hard, so loosen the base with a small tool first.
Keep grazing animals away from seeding patches, so they do not carry the seeds into clean fields.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Grasses

If water and weeding cannot hold goosegrass down, choose an active ingredient that works on grasses at the age of your rice. The table follows PhilRice recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before the seed heads open, and clean the thresher and harvester before they enter the field.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [grass weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. Anee tells you which weed it most likely is, its group, and what to do at the age of your rice. You can also put the weeding days on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar), so the team knows when to go in.

items.q: What are the local names of goosegrass?
items.a: This grass has more local names than most weeds. You may hear bakis bakisan, bang angan, bikad bikad, bila bila, palagtiki, parangis, paragis, sabung sabungan or sambali. Its scientific name is Eleusine indica. Since names change from town to town, check for the whitish, flat stem base and the 3 to 6 finger spikes to be sure.

items.q: How do I control this grass in my rice field?
items.a: Start by keeping the bunds and paths clean, so it cannot seed into the paddy. Keep water standing when you can, since it prefers drier soil. Then hand weed early, before the spikes ripen. If you still need a herbicide, choose one for grass weeds that fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Can animals eat it, and is that a problem?
items.a: Animals do eat it, and that is part of the problem. Its seeds spread easily when animals eat the seed heads, so grazing animals can carry them to clean fields. Keep your animals off seeding patches, or cut the patch before the spikes ripen. That way the seeds stay out of your paddy and your next crop starts cleaner.
